name: Drug-induced / toxic hepatitis

matching.reasoningTemplate: Jaundice and transaminitis after a hepatotoxic drug/overdose, without sepsis, suggests toxic hepatitis.

redFlags: Acute liver failure (coagulopathy + encephalopathy) → transplant referral

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e, Chapter 351 (Toxic and Drug-Induced Hepatitis), pp.2665-2672; anti-TB hepatotoxicity monitoring p.1463; liver transplantation/ALF context Chapter 356 pp.2718-2719
clinicalPearls: DILI is the most common cause of acute liver failure, and signals of hepatotoxicity in clinical trials are the leading reason candidate drugs fail to reach approval (p.2665).

Two broad mechanisms are recognised: direct (intrinsic) toxicity that is predictable and dose-dependent with a short latency, versus idiosyncratic reactions that are infrequent (roughly 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 100,000), unpredictable, and may appear at any time but typically 5-90 days after starting the drug (p.2665, p.2667).

Although idiosyncratic injury is regarded as not dose-related, most implicated drugs are given at relatively high daily doses (often >100 mg); high-potency drugs given in milligram amounts rarely cause hepatotoxicity (p.2665).

The hepatocellular-versus-cholestatic pattern is defined by the R value, the ratio of ALT to alkaline phosphatase (each as multiples of the upper limit of normal): R >5.0 = hepatocellular, R <2.0 = cholestatic, R 2.0-5.0 = mixed (p.2667).

Hy's Law (named for Hyman Zimmerman): the appearance of jaundice during drug therapy predicts more serious injury, with roughly a 10:1 ratio of jaundiced cases to acute liver failure (about 1 in 10 jaundiced patients progresses to liver failure) (p.2667).

Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) is the most frequently implicated single antibiotic/agent causing DILI in the US and Europe, typically producing mixed or predominantly cholestatic injury that may begin after the drug has already been stopped (p.2667, p.2670).
Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is the prototype direct hepatotoxin and the most prevalent cause of acute liver failure in the Western world (p.2667, p.2668).

A characteristic biochemical signature of acetaminophen injury is very high aminotransferases (often >10,000 IU/L, far above viral hepatitis) with relatively low bilirubin in the hyperacute phase; this should prompt focused questioning even without a clear overdose history (p.2668).
Complementary and alternative (herbal/dietary) medicines now account for over 20% of DILI in the US; weight-loss products and anabolic steroids are common culprits and are often unregulated (p.2671).

Acetaminophen toxicity is potentiated by chronic alcohol use (CYP2E1 induction plus glutathione depletion), so the toxic dose may be as low as ~2 g in chronic alcoholics; starvation/fasting and enzyme-inducing drugs (phenobarbital, isoniazid) also increase susceptibility (p.2668-2670).
Four agents are notable for causing a chronic, autoimmune-hepatitis-like picture with positive ANA: nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, and alpha-methyldopa (p.2667, p.2670).

DILI is nearly always a presumptive diagnosis of exclusion; causality assessment relies on temporal association, injury pattern, the drug's prior record, and ruling out other causes (scoring tools: RUCAM, DILIN expert opinion, newer RECAM) (p.2667-2668).

Drug hepatotoxicity is generally not more frequent in those with pre-existing chronic liver disease, although the severity of outcome may be greater; statins specifically can be used safely in chronic hepatitis C and steatosis (p.2668, p.2671-2672).
harrison.pathophysiology: Liver injury can follow ingestion of essentially any xenobiotic (industrial toxins, drugs, herbal/dietary supplements). Most drugs are lipophilic and undergo phase I oxidation/methylation by cytochrome P450 enzymes followed by phase II conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation) or glutathione inactivation to a water-soluble form for renal/biliary excretion; most hepatotoxicity arises from a reactive phase I metabolite, and glutathione depletion compounds the injury. Damage occurs through several overlapping routes: direct hepatocyte injury via free radicals/reactive intermediates causing membrane lipid peroxidation; activation of innate or adaptive immune responses (HLA-haplotype-dependent hapten binding, cytotoxic lymphocytes, antibody-mediated cytotoxicity); triggering of apoptosis via TNF-alpha/Fas pathways; disruption of bile canalicular transport pumps (e.g., MRP3) leading to toxic bile-acid accumulation and cholestasis; and inhibition of mitochondrial beta-oxidation/respiration producing lactic acidosis and microvesicular steatosis. Nuclear receptors such as CAR and PXR can also induce hepatotoxicity. For acetaminophen specifically, a minor fraction is converted by CYP2E1 to the reactive metabolite NAPQI, normally detoxified by conjugation with hepatoprotective glutathione; when NAPQI overwhelms or glutathione is depleted, NAPQI binds covalently to hepatocyte macromolecules forming protein adducts that drive centrilobular necrosis.
additionalDifferentials: Viral hepatitis (idiosyncratic DILI from isoniazid or ciprofloxacin can be clinically and histologically indistinguishable from acute hepatitis A/B/C) (p.2667)
Autoimmune hepatitis (nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, methyldopa produce an AIH-like picture with positive ANA) (p.2667, p.2670)
Alcohol-associated (alcoholic) hepatitis (amiodarone causes a pseudoalcoholic injury with steatosis, neutrophilic infiltration, and Mallory's hyaline) (p.2670)
Primary sclerosing cholangitis (a PSC-like picture can follow chemotherapy and long-term ketamine use) (p.2667)
Primary biliary cholangitis-like lesion (rarely associated with chlorpromazine) (p.2669)
infectionMimics: Acute viral hepatitis A, B, or C (hepatocellular idiosyncratic DILI mimics it; differentiate with viral serologies) (p.2667)
nonInfectiousMimics: Ischemic (hypoxic) hepatitis and other causes of marked transaminase elevation (p.2668)
Cholestasis of pregnancy / estrogen-induced cholestasis (genetically determined canalicular transporter defects) (p.2667)

Budd-Chiari syndrome / hepatic vein occlusion and venoocclusive (sinusoidal obstruction) disease as drug-related vascular mimics (oral contraceptives; pyrrolizidine alkaloids; pre-transplant chemotherapy) (p.2667, p.2670, p.2671)
additionalInvestigations: Calculate the R value (ALT/ALP, each as multiples of ULN) to classify hepatocellular vs cholestatic vs mixed injury (p.2667)
Detailed exposure history including occupational/home chemicals, prescription and OTC drugs, and herbal/dietary supplements (p.2665, p.2671)

Serum acetaminophen level interpreted against the time-based nomogram (levels 4-8 h post-ingestion guide risk; >300 ug/mL at 4 h predicts severe injury, <150 ug/mL makes injury highly unlikely) (p.2668, p.2670)
Viral hepatitis serologies and autoantibodies (ANA, anti-smooth muscle, anti-mitochondrial, anti-LKM2) to exclude/identify autoimmune-pattern DILI (p.2667, p.2670)
Eosinophil count (eosinophilia supports a hypersensitivity reaction, e.g., trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, phenytoin) (p.2665, p.2671)
Liver biopsy where the pattern is unclear (helps distinguish injury types; e.g., electron microscopy showing phospholipid-laden lamellar bodies in amiodarone toxicity) (p.2670)
Arterial lactate in severe acetaminophen injury (>3.5 mmol/L identifies patients much more likely to need transplantation) (p.2670)
Causality assessment tools (RUCAM, DILIN structured expert opinion, RECAM) and reference resources (LiverTox) (p.2668)
redFlags: Jaundice arising during drug therapy (Hy's Law) - predicts severe injury and a substantial risk of progression to liver failure (p.2667)
Rising aminotransferases to >5x the upper limit of normal (or >3x ULN with symptoms) - threshold to withdraw the suspected agent (p.2668)
Acute liver failure features: coagulopathy plus hepatic encephalopathy; develops in ~10% of DILI cases (p.2668)
Cerebral edema in progressing acute liver failure (p.2667, Chap.356)
Acute kidney injury and myocardial injury accompanying severe acetaminophen toxicity (renal injury in ~75% of severe cases) (p.2668, p.2670)
Lactic acidosis (mitochondrial toxicity, e.g., with nucleoside analogues/antiretrovirals or valproate) (p.2665, p.2672)
Hypersensitivity/DRESS features (rash, fever, eosinophilia) accompanying liver injury (e.g., trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) (p.2671)
Continued use of the offending agent despite symptoms - most fatalities (e.g., isoniazid) occur in this setting (p.2668, p.2670)
harrison.prognosis: Most DILI is self-limited and resolves after the offending agent is withdrawn. However, acute liver failure develops in about 10% of DILI cases; once that threshold (coagulopathy plus hepatic encephalopathy) is reached, spontaneous recovery occurs in fewer than 30%, and liver transplantation is undertaken in more than 40% of these patients (p.2668). For acetaminophen, up to 72% of poisoned patients in some Scandinavian series progress to encephalopathy and coagulopathy (lower in the UK/US); a single dose of 10-15 g can cause clinical injury and fulminant fatal disease is usually associated with >=25 g; the N-acetylcysteine antidote markedly reduces severity and is most effective given early (within ~8-12 h), though it retains some benefit up to 24-36 h. Survivors of acetaminophen overdose rarely have ongoing liver injury (p.2668, p.2670). Several agents cause chronic injury or progression to cirrhosis (methotrexate, tamoxifen, amiodarone), and the autoimmune-pattern agents (nitrofurantoin, minocycline, hydralazine, methyldopa) can lead to cirrhosis if not recognised early (p.2668-2670).
pitfalls: Treating mild, transient aminotransferase rises ('adaptation', e.g., with isoniazid, valproate, phenytoin, statins) as significant injury - these often resolve despite continued use; conversely, ignoring symptomatic/progressive rises is dangerous (p.2665, p.2669, p.2671-2672).

Missing the acetaminophen diagnosis because of denial, altered mentation, or staggered/unintentional overdose - very high transaminases with low bilirubin should raise suspicion even without a clear history (p.2668).
Forgetting herbal/dietary supplements and OTC products in the drug history - they now cause >20% of US DILI and may contain undeclared chemicals (e.g., diclofenac in 'antirheumatic herbs') (p.2671).
Assuming standard acetaminophen doses are safe in chronic alcohol users - the toxic threshold can fall to ~2 g (p.2670).
Attributing cholestatic jaundice in a young male body-builder to hepatitis rather than anabolic/androgenic steroid use (p.2670).
Expecting injury only early in therapy - amoxicillin-clavulanate and nitrofurantoin can have long latency and may declare after the drug is stopped (p.2670).
In direct toxins, focusing on the liver while missing concurrent renal or other organ involvement that may threaten survival (p.2668).
harrison.severityClassification: Injury pattern is classified by the R value (ALT/ALP as multiples of ULN): R >5.0 hepatocellular, R <2.0 cholestatic, R 2.0-5.0 mixed (p.2667). Hy's Law serves as a severity/prognostic marker: jaundice (significant bilirubin rise) accompanying hepatocellular DILI predicts a markedly higher risk of acute liver failure (about a 10:1 jaundice-to-failure ratio) (p.2667). The aminotransferase threshold of >5x ULN (or >3x ULN with symptoms) marks the point at which the offending agent should be withdrawn (p.2668). Causality (not severity) is graded on a five-point likelihood scale by DILIN (definite, highly likely, probable, possible, unlikely) (p.2668). The clinical endpoint of severity is acute liver failure, defined by coagulopathy plus hepatic encephalopathy (p.2668).
